<reflection>
The first experiment provided a baseline with moderate substrate (2.0 M) and catalyst (0.01 M). The fitting results show that M20 is a clear outlier with a much higher NLL (-6.49) compared to the other mechanisms (around -22 to -23), indicating it fits poorly and can be considered implausible. However, the remaining 19 mechanisms have NLL values very close together (differences <1), meaning the single experiment does not provide sufficient discrimination among them. The aim of the first turn was to establish a baseline, which was achieved, but further experiments are needed to reduce uncertainty across the large set of plausible mechanisms.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To discriminate among the 19 remaining mechanisms, we need to probe catalyst concentration dependence. Many mechanisms involve catalyst dimerization (M2, M3, M5), deactivation steps that may depend on catalyst concentration (M9, M13, M14, etc.), or other catalyst-speciation events. By reducing the catalyst concentration by an order of magnitude (from 0.01 M to 0.001 M) while keeping substrate constant (2.0 M) and no initial product, we can test whether the kinetics scale linearly with catalyst or show nonlinear behavior. This condition is not extreme (still within the allowed range) and should yield measurable rates. Mechanisms with dimerization or bimolecular catalyst steps will exhibit different scaling compared to simple first-order-in-catalyst mechanisms. Additionally, deactivation pathways may have different relative impacts at low catalyst. This design avoids repeating similar regimes and targets multiple mechanism classes simultaneously, rather than focusing on a single pair.
</hypothesis>
